newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour would keep clamp on spending - Brown.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour would keep clamp on spending - Brown.

text.p: Economics spokesman for Britain's main opposition Labour Party, Gordon Brown, will state that Labour would want budget savings before reallocating resources.

This, together with a restatement of Labour's new promise of a referendum if, once in power, it decided to take Britain into a single European currency, will be the key promises in a speech to traders on Tuesday night, sources in Brown's office said.

Brown will tell the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE): "In government we will begin by looking for savings within existing budgets as we reallocate resources to meet the proper priorities for Britain."
The speech comes after Brown's weekend pledge of a referendum on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) if a Labour government decided to enter a single currency.
The pledge is seen as an acknowledgement that Labour is cooling on the prospect of early entry into EMU, although Brown himself remains in favour of early entry.
Brown is expected to say that Labour is keeping open its options on a single currency.
But he will call Labour's position clear and principled in contrast to what he will describe as the prevaricating of the ruling Conservatives, who are chronically split on Europe.
But the key point expected to be highlighted by British newspapers on Wednesday is Brown's promise of tight fiscal management under a Labour government.

Brown is expected to promise "a budget for stability that will set a tough inflation target and tough fiscal rules and, unlike under the present administration, it will be a budget that ensures that both will be met".
In addition to the promise to seek budget savings before reallocating public resources, Brown is also expected to hint at a drive to raise investment levels.
Brown is expected to repeat pledges to move people from welfare to education and to restate plans for a windfall tax on recently privatised utilities to pay for welfare reform.

Brown is also expected to repeat Labour's promise to cut Value Added Tax on fuel and to attack Conservative plans for the abolition of capital gains tax and inheritance tax as proposals which would benefit the few rather than the many.
